units.text: Amazon R D S is a managed service for running a relational database. A relational database keeps structured data in tables that an app can query with S Q L. Think of an online store where a customer wants to check an order status. The store app connects to its R D S database endpoint. In this example the database engine is PostgreSQL. The app asks PostgreSQL for the matching order, and the database sends back the status.

The database engine still runs the query. R D S handles much of the work of running the database, like provisioning the infrastructure, applying patches, and taking automated backups when configured. You still decide what the tables look like, write and tune queries, and control access.
Use R D S when your application needs a familiar relational database, but you don't want to operate the underlying database server yourself.

Amazon Aurora is a managed relational database with MySQL-compatible and PostgreSQL-compatible editions. Use it when your app needs S Q L and you want to scale read work separately from writes. Think of a store that needs to save receipts as customers check out. Those writes go to the Aurora writer. Now imagine the reporting app asking for totals from receipts already saved.

An optional Aurora reader can handle those reads, so the writer can concentrate on new orders. The writer and readers are separate pieces of compute, but they use the same distributed cluster storage across Availability Zones. Adding a reader adds read capacity rather than a whole new copy of that storage for each instance. Reports that need the very latest write should account for possible reader lag.
Choose the compatible edition your app needs and test the features it relies on.

Amazon DynamoDB is a managed database for looking up items by key. It works well when you know how your app will ask for its data. Imagine a game app opening the racing score for Player 42. The partition key identifies the player, and the sort key in this table identifies the game. Together, Player 42 and Racing identify one item, whose score is 900.

Puzzle is a different item under the same player, with a different sort key. Those two items can have different non-key attributes: Racing might store a best lap, while Puzzle might store a level. The keys are still required. Think first about what the player screen needs to read, then choose keys that support those requests without searching the whole table.
That's the main difference between designing this table for the app and just collecting every score in one place.
